summary: High-stayed videos (66%+ stayed) use short Hinglish question titles ending with relevant emojis rather than long, academic English/Hindi titles. Winning hooks immediately start with an active counter-intuitive claim or a vivid personal visualization ('सोचो... / तुम्हें...'). High-performing topics combine extreme comparisons (e.g., T. rex vs. cars, car crash physics) with everyday relatable objects. Longer, textbook-style scripts (>40s with academic language) drop retention below 37% stayed and under 100 views. Structuring hooks around physical, tangible metaphors ('3 cars on your teeth') drives initial retention past the critical 60% threshold.
winning_hooks: Start immediately with direct second-person framing ('तुम / तुम्हें / तुम्हारे') paired with extreme visual imagery.
Present a bold counter-intuitive fact in sentence one ('जो car crash में पिचक जाती है, वो तुम्हें ज़्यादा बचाती है').
Use everyday objects for scale comparison in the first 3 seconds (e.g., comparing bite force to stacking 3 cars on teeth).
avoid: Avoid formal/documentary Hindi or English sentence structures (e.g., 'जीवाश्मों में वैज्ञानिकों को ऐसी सूक्ष्म आकृतियां...').
Avoid descriptive title-style opening statements that state facts without personal stakes or curiosity gaps.
Avoid standard-length (>40s) explanatory scripts that lack mid-video visual/narrative pivots.
next_experiment: A/B test a single topic ('Why airplane windows are round') with two different hook styles: Option A using direct personal scale ('सोचो, अगर प्लेन की खिड़कियां चौकोर होतीं तो उड़ते ही फट जातीं...') vs Option B using standard documentary narration ('विमानों की खिड़कियां गोल क्यों बनाई जाती हैं?'). Measure difference in stayed_pct.
